deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics. It is a page of Riemann's reading notes (excerpts and paraphrase) from Herbart's essay "Über Kategorien und Conjunctionen", which the heading cites as Werke (Hartenstein edition) Bd. VII. That essay is in Herbart's Psychologische Untersuchungen. The page refers to Herbart's §§ 59, 62, 63 and to p. 545. It continues the excerpts on the previous page (§§ 69-70, W. VII pp. 556-560). There are no derivations to restate. The content is as follows.

(1) Conjunctions versus categories. Conjunctions are forms of linking thoughts in language. Aristotle looked in language for categories as concepts of cognition ('Erkenntnissbegriffe'). Kant's categories are the transition between the two: they are meant to be concepts of cognition, but also forms of combination. In how they are obtained they are opposed to Aristotle's.

(2) Riemann copies Aristotle, Categories 2 (1a16-19) and 4 (1b25-27). Of things said, some are said in combination (κατὰ συμπλοκήν, e.g. 'man runs') and some without combination (e.g. 'man', 'ox', 'runs'). Each uncombined term signifies one of: substance, quantity, quality, relation, where, when, position, having, acting, being acted upon. Herbart's point is that Aristotle expressly sets the judgment form aside. Kant instead derives his categories from the table of judgments (quantity, quality, relation, modality).

(3) A cross-reference to Herbart, Psychologie § 124, on categories as concepts of cognition. Herbart argues that the only premise Kant and Aristotle share is that the categories are concepts of cognition. Otherwise Aristotle could equally have counted the predicables of the Topics, or aesthetic class concepts (beautiful, ugly, good, evil), among the categories. Here Riemann adds his own bracketed remark, signed 'R.': 'Could Aristotle not count these under ποιόν [quality]?'

(4) Excerpt from VII p. 545, § 63, on Herbart's four main categories. The machine transcription reads 'Ding, Eigenschaft, Verhältniss, Veränderung'; Herbart's own list is thing, property, relation, the negated ('Verneintes'). Herbart's argument:
- οὐσία stays at the head, as in Aristotle, because cognition presupposes an object.
- Then comes the most general judgment form, the attachment of a predicate to a subject, which judgment shares even with the question.
- What distinguishes judgment from question is Yes/No, and the No gives the category of the negated.
- A predicate attributed to an object taken by itself gives 'property'.
- A predicate that holds only when the object is grasped together with others, and lapses when that grouping lapses, gives 'relation'. Strictly, relation rests on conditional negation, which is why property and relation can be set against each other.

(5) A fragmentary footnote-style addition, partly illegible. Comparisons of magnitude still occur even where no metric is available: one cannot measure a time span in feet and inches, or give a sound interval as a fixed size. A difference of colours or shapes can serve as a yardstick for other, similar, larger or smaller differences, since only comparisons and relations matter.

results.what: Excerpt/paraphrase of Herbart's discussion of Aristotle's ten categories versus Kant's categories derived from judgment forms, and of Herbart's own four categories (thing, property, relation, the negated)
results.modern_name: History of category theory in philosophy (Aristotle, Kant, Herbart)
results.usually_credited_to: Johann Friedrich Herbart, 'Über Kategorien und Conjunctionen' (Psychologische Untersuchungen, c. 1839-40)

results.what: Riemann's marginal query whether Aristotle could have placed aesthetic and evaluative concepts under the category of quality (ποιόν)
results.modern_name: Philosophical remark on the scope of the category of quality

deep.surprise_reason: These are purely philosophical reading notes on Herbart and Aristotle, with one short query of Riemann's own. Riemann's study of Herbart is well documented, and there is no mathematical content.
transcription_corrections: Line 3: 'denn Anschein nach ganz verschiedene Dinge' should read 'dem Anschein nach ganz verschiedene Dinge'.

§63 list of the four main categories: the item read as 'Veränderung' after 'Verhältniss' is very likely 'Verneintes' (or 'Verneinung'), matching Herbart's four categories Ding, Eigenschaft, Verhältniss, Verneintes. The crossed-out word is probably also a form of 'Verneinung'.
'Das Nein aber liegt in der Kategorie des Veränderlichen' should most likely read 'in der Kategorie des Verneinten'.
'wo sie auch dem Verneinten, Getadelten[?], Verbotenen' likely reads 'wo es mit dem Verneinten, Getadelten, Verbotenen einerlei Grund und Boden hat'; the start of the clause is uncertain.
The line 'Dinge[?] hat Aristoteles in der letzten[?]' is probably a heading for the footnote; the reading is uncertain, possibly 'Dies hat Aristoteles in der Logik'.
The Greek quotation matches Aristotle, Categories 1a16-19 and 1b25-27. The breathings and accents in the machine transcription (e.g. ποσόν, ποιόν, πού, ποτέ) are acceptable.
